subtitle: Presenting a topic in structure, and switching between formal and plain
words.intro: Applying for German citizenship takes a test, a language certificate and a ceremony with a mayor. Maya has been asked to give a short talk at hers, in front of the whole town hall. She’s been told to keep it simple.

grammar[0].fact: A German talk is expected to have a *Gliederung*, an outline, often on the first slide. You say what you’ll say, you say it, and you say that you said it. It’s not exciting. It does mean that nobody’s ever lost.

grammar[1].fact: The national naturalisation test asks 33 questions from a public list of 300. You can practise online for nothing. Quite a few people born in Germany have tried it for fun, and not all of them have passed.

document.intro: A real certificate of naturalisation from Wiesbaden. The woman named on it was born in Germany in 1910, and in 1958 she lived in Israel. Read the dates and the two places. Then consider what lies between them.
document.fact: Article 116 of the Basic Law gives people who lost their German citizenship between 1933 and 1945 on political, racial or religious grounds, and their descendants, the right to get it back on application. Thousands still apply each year. The fee on this certificate reads: *frei*.

reading.intro: A Friday in the town hall. Fourteen new citizens, one mayor, a flag and a trolley with sparkling wine. Maya has prepared ten minutes, on index cards. Everyone she knows is in the second row. She begins, as she was taught. Then she drops the cards.
reading.fact: German naturalisation ceremonies are organised by each town and vary from a handshake in a side room to a brass band. New citizens often sing the national anthem from a printed sheet. The third verse is the only one sung, the first having become unsayable. They now get to vote, sit on a jury, and be asked for directions.
